title: Profiling tooling and scripts runbook v7
body:
Summary:
This runbook documents the profiling tooling, scripts, and CI jobs we use to find latency and throughput regressions in the serving runtime. It covers CI job layout, local capture recipes, flamegraph generation for CPU workloads, GPU trace capture with Nsight Systems (nsys), common regressions and how to triage, and links to automation scripts. Intended audience: eng-serving-runtime and performance-focused SREs.

Scope and goals:
- Detect and alert on performance regressions early (CI + nightly perf jobs).
- Provide reproducible trace capture recipes for CPU and GPU stacks.
- Standardize flamegraph generation and interpretation.
- Document root-cause checklist for common performance regressions.

Where code lives (repo paths):
- perf CI workflow: .github/workflows/perf-ci.yml
- perf runner scripts: infra/ci/perf/run_perf_bench.sh
- flamegraph helpers and collapse scripts: tools/perf/flamegraph/*.pl (Brendan Gregg scripts + wrappers)
- nsight/collector helpers: tools/perf/nsys_collect.sh
- perf postprocessing: tools/perf/postprocess/*.py

Perf CI job overview (high level):
- Purpose: run a stable set of benchmarks on a controlled runner to catch regressions.
- Schedule: nightly and PR-gated for large changes touching scheduling, batching, or kernels.
- Runners: self-hosted runners tagged perf-gpu-x86 and perf-cpu-x86 with pinned hardware images.
- Artifacts: raw traces (perf.data, nsys-rep), flamegraphs (svg), summarized CSV metrics uploaded to s3.
- Thresholds: per-benchmark latency P95 and tokens/sec baseline with +/- allowed drift. If drift > 7% (configurable) CI fails and posts a failure artifact link.

Key CI job config snippets (example, see repo for full file):
- .github/workflows/perf-ci.yml triggers:
  - on: [pull_request] for paths: ["serving_runtime/**", "infra/**"] (heavy PRs)
  - on: schedule: cron: '0 6 * * *' (nightly global run)
- job steps: checkout, setup-runner (install perf, nsys, python deps), build-bench-image, run-bench (runs run_perf_bench.sh), upload-artifacts (to s3).

Local capture recipes (CPU):
1) Build with debug symbols and optimizations preserved: make build RELWITHDEBINFO=1
2) Run the target with representative workload: ./build/bin/serve_bench --model=resnet50 --seq-len=512 --batch-size=1 --num-requests=5000
3) Capture using perf: sudo perf record -F 99 -g -o perf.data -- ./build/bin/serve_bench --model=resnet50 ...
4) Convert to folded stacks and flamegraph: sudo perf script -i perf.data | ./tools/perf/flamegraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
   ./tools/perf/flamegraph/flamegraph.pl out.folded > flame.svg
5) Open flame.svg and look for wide stacks (hot paths), especially in runtime::generate_token, attention kernels, and memcpy calls.

Local GPU capture recipes (Nsight Systems):
1) Use nsys (preferred for mixed CPU+CUDA tracing):
   nsys profile --output=bench --trace=cuda,cudnn,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-end=stop -- ./build/bin/serve_bench --model=tiny-transformer --seq-len=1024 --batch-size=1
2) After capture: nsys stats bench.qdrep --report gputrace --format=csv > nsys_gputrace.csv
   nsys export --output=bench.sqlite --format=sqlite bench.qdrep (for UI share)
3) Convert nsys API stacks to flamegraphs (we use a custom adapter):
   python tools/perf/postprocess/nsys_to_collapsed.py --input bench.qdrep --output bench.folded
   ./tools/perf/flamegraph/flamegraph.pl bench.folded > gpu_flame.svg
Note: GPU flamegraphs show time per API/kernels and are useful to spot repeated kernel invocation overhead vs long kernel execution.

Using NVIDIA Nsight Compute (ncu) for kernel-level bottlenecks:
- Run targeted kernel profiling: ncu --kernel-id-metrics -o kernel_report ./build/bin/serve_bench --model=...
- Look at achieved occupancy, memory throughput, and SM efficiency. High stalls on memory or serialization often point to suboptimal kernel selection or inefficient CUDA memory copies.

Common commands quick reference:
- perf record: sudo perf record -F 99 -g -o perf.data -- <cmd>
- perf report: sudo perf report -i perf.data
- perf script -> flamegraph: sudo perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > flame.svg
- nsys capture: nsys profile --output=run --trace=cuda,osrt -- <cmd>
- nsys stats: nsys stats run.qdrep --report gputrace --format=csv
- ncu: ncu -o report --target-processes all --set full <cmd>

Postmortem triage checklist (if CI shows regression):
1) Validate reproducibility: rerun the exact CI job image locally (or on perf runner) and re-capture traces.
2) Compare flamegraphs between baseline and regression run: look for new wide stacks or growing call times.
3) Check batch/sequence distribution: verify test harness didn't change input distribution (KV cache misses, longer sequences increase kernel work).
4) Inspect scheduling/batching metrics: verify batching latency vs throughput tradeoffs.
5) GPU: check for kernel fallback to slower implementation (e.g., fallback to F32 from F16/quantized path) or increased memcpy times.
6) Inspect CPU-side hotspots: serialization, argument marshalling, logging, mutex contention. Use perf top + flamegraph.
7) If kernel-level suspicion: capture ncu and look at SM utilization and memory-bound stalls.
8) Check upstream dependencies and recent PRs (linked PRs are in linked_artifacts).
9) If not obvious, escalate to perf-analysts (add label perf-investigation, assign to eng-serving-runtime rotation).

Interpreting flamegraphs (rules of thumb):
- Tall wide boxes at leaf nodes = hot functions (focus here).
- Long stacks with small leaf width indicate repeated short calls (overhead). Consider batching or inlining.
- High time in memcpy/memset indicates copy overhead; consider zero-copy paths or pinned memory.
- Many small kernels on GPU may indicate poor kernel fusion; prefer fewer larger kernels.

Automated baselining and regression detection:
- We store nightly CSV summaries in s3 with metrics: test_name, median_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, tokens_per_sec.
- A simple regression detector compares moving average of the last 7 runs vs current. If drift > threshold, it opens JIRA INF-REGRESS (templated) and uploads perf artifacts.
- Tools: tools/perf/compare_baselines.py and infra/ci/perf/regression_alerts.py

Debugging examples (real past incidents):
- Case 1: 2025-08-11 regression in seq=4096 paths. Root cause: kernel selector fell back from fused attention to non-fused due to a boundary-check bug. Fix was in PR #421 (linked).
- Case 2: 2025-10-02 nightly drift: increased CPU time in argument marshalling after adding detailed logging in request path. Fix: reduce log verbosity behind a flag + defer JSON serialization.

Best practices and tips:
- Always preserve debug symbols for nightly runs (RELWITHDEBINFO). Stripped builds hide useful symbols.
- Reproduce on identical hardware. Different CPU microarchitectures and driver versions can change kernel selection.
- Keep trace sizes manageable: sample frequency 99 Hz for perf is usually enough; for heavy noisy systems lower sampling.
- Annotate code with NVTX ranges around critical sections; makes nsys traces much easier to collapse and reason about.
- Record metadata with artifacts (git sha, docker image id, driver versions, CUDA version).

Operational notes for perf runners:
- Runner setup script: infra/ci/perf/setup_runner.sh installs perf, linux-tools, nsys, ncu, python deps, and configures NVIDIA driver pinned to approved versions.
- Retention: raw traces kept 30 days, summarized CSV and flamegraphs kept 90 days.
- Access: artifacts uploaded to s3 bucket redwood-perf-artifacts with IAM roles for perf team.

Appendix: quick links and references:
- Flamegraph scripts: https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph
- Nsight Systems docs: https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-systems/
- Perf man page: https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/trace/perf.html
- Relevant PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/421
- Triage template (Confluence): confluence:SERVING-RUNTIME-PROFILING

Contact and on-call rotation:
- Perf on-call (eng-serving-runtime): see #perf-oncall Slack channel.
- Primary contact for this runbook: Samantha Lee (owner).

Unresolved / TODOs:
- Add automated GPU flamegraph diffing tooling (open ticket: INF-4678).
- Integrate nsys -> folded stack converter upstream so CI can generate GPU flamegraphs without postprocess VM step.

Notes to self (informal):
- We still have noisy variance from autoscaling on shared perf runners; consider dedicated isolated hosts for final verification.
- For very long sequences the nvtx windowing becomes important (capture-range).
